Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Arthur Vance was seventy-four now, but the mornings still began with the same careful inventory of his body. For decades, his life had been defined by the wide, wind-blown tarmac of his career as a combat pilot, but the threat had never lived in the cockpit. It had arrived in the quiet house he shared with his wife, a woman whose hands could be steady and gentle until they turned. The physical abuse was never theatrical; it was a steady accumulation of force. A palm slammed against his chest, fingers closing too tight around his upper arm, a heel catching his shin as he walked past her in the kitchen. Arthur never allowed himself to feel or express anger during those encounters. He had come to believe that speaking up or pushing back would only invite more force, so he simply stood still, swallowing the heat until it settled in his jaw. Now, even though he was widowed, the physical touch of a hand on his shoulder still made his muscles lock and his breath catch. What frightened him most was the suddenness of the sensation, how a light graze from a neighbor could send a jolt of physical reactivity through his entire frame. He spent his weekdays at the regional aviation hangar, reviewing flight manifests and advising younger pilots. It was a space of controlled skies, yet avoidance had quietly carved out the edges of his routine. He left the hangar before lunch whenever he knew the offender would come for a visit, because seeing the person who harmed him, with her familiar sharp cheekbones and knowing tilt, was enough to make Arthur step into the shadows of the supply corridor. He avoided the kitchen area where she had often stood, and he kept his distance from the pilot’s lounge where men leaned in too close to share stories. At home, the olfactory trigger lay dormant in the medicine cabinet until the first whiff of her alcohol on his worn flight jacket would suddenly pull him back. The alcohol smell would rise like a weight, and his heart would begin to drum against his ribs. He had learned to leave the jacket in the garage, and when he saw the bottle on the counter, he would carefully set it aside, noting how the familiar scent lingered in the air. The years had layered his vigilance into a constant state of watchfulness. Even at rest, Arthur remained superalert, his eyes tracking the door, his head on a slow swivel, always ready to register a shift in the room. This watchfulness followed him into the night. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert; he would lie rigid under the sheets, listening to the house settle, certain that silence was merely the pause before movement. He avoided the deep sleep that used to come so naturally, treating rest as a temporary lowering of defenses that could not be sustained. With his wife gone, he had expected his life to open, yet he found himself avoiding intimacy, keeping emotional closeness at a careful distance. He would nod politely at conversations, accept visits, but he never allowed himself to lean in, never let his guard drop enough to share what he carried. The anger he had suppressed for decades still rested quietly beneath his ribs, a dense, unacknowledged presence that he simply refused to name. What finally brought Arthur to seek help was not a single crisis, but the slow accumulation of his own habits. He noticed how he no longer sat through a full meal, how he flinched when a barista’s hand brushed his when handing over a cup, how he had stopped visiting the old neighborhood because every porch light felt like a signal. He was certain that if he allowed himself to relax, even for an hour, the old tensions would return. Yet he hoped, as he sat in the clinic with its low ceiling and predictable routines, that someone might help him separate the present from the past. He did not need the anger released or the memories rewritten; he simply needed to breathe easier in a world that no longer felt so ready to strike.
